title: Hairdressers
strapline: Just a trim? Rollers, spray bottles and the best chat in the room.
intent: The salon is built on conversation — the mirror chat, 'going anywhere nice?', the running commentary of a stylist at work.
Brushing, styling, spraying and clipping demand delicate hand control: rollers to wind, clips to pinch open, bottles to squeeze and pump.
Doing someone's hair means touching gently and checking they're comfortable — care and consent, practised daily.
Hair itself opens the door to difference: curls, braids, locs, head coverings — every head in our community is different, and different is interesting.
The appointment book, price list and loyalty cards keep purposeful print and mark-making at the front desk.
Waiting your turn with a magazine is queuing at its most civilised.
implementation: Sit in the chair yourself and be the chattiest customer in Ealing — the mirror conversation is the language goldmine here.
Model the stylist's gentle running commentary: 'I'm just going to brush the ends — tell me if that pulls.'
Stock the salon for every kind of hair: wide-tooth combs, bobbles, headscarves, dolls and photos showing many hair types and styles.
Talk about hair difference with warm curiosity, never comparison — 'look how your curls spring back! Whose hair at home is like yours?'
Put the appointment book, price list and a phone at reception, and let the receptionist run the bookings.
Add water spray bottles and real (empty) product bottles — pumping and squeezing is quiet hand-gym.
Coach the consent habit: always ask before touching anyone's hair, and stop when asked.
key_questions: What would you like today — just a trim, or something new?
How does it feel when someone brushes your hair gently?
Whose hair in your family is like yours? Whose is different?
Who's booked in next — what does the appointment book say?
What do you need to ask before you start on someone's hair?

impact.text: Children replay salon scenes — washing, styling, the big reveal in the mirror — and sustain them with shared roles of stylist, receptionist and customer.
Stylist and customer keep a genuine mirror conversation going across many turns — holidays, birthdays, what the dog did.
Children wind rollers, pinch clips open, squeeze spray bottles and wield brushes with careful, deliberate control.
Children touch gently, ask first and check their customer is comfortable — kindness as a working habit.
Children notice and talk warmly about different hair, styles and coverings in their setting and community — different is interesting, not wrong.
Children 'write' appointments in the book and prices on the list, and read them back to callers.
Children wait their turn in the salon chairs, magazine in hand, increasingly gracefully.

enhancements: A real hand mirror and a safe wall mirror at child height — the reveal is half the play.
Wide-tooth combs, soft brushes, bobbles, clips and headscarves for every hair type.
Empty (washed) shampoo and product bottles from families' own bathrooms.
Water spray bottles for a proper wet-look styling session on the dolls.
An appointment book, phone and price list at the reception desk.
Photo cards of many hairstyles — braids, locs, fades, buns — for customers to choose from.
A barber's day: clippers (pretend), a striped pole picture and gowns.

playing_exploring: Children replay an experience full of sensation — water, brushing, the chair that pumps up — from the powerful side of the scissors.
Bottles, clips and rollers each demand their own investigation before the salon opens.
active_learning: A style started must be finished for the mirror reveal — children persist through fiddly clips and uncooperative bobbles.
creating_thinking: Children invent styles, name them, and adapt when the rollers won't hold — creativity you can wear.
